answer:
**Unlabeled data help only when their structure supports a valid learning assumption.** Label propagation assumes nearby graph nodes tend to share labels. Pseudo-labeling assumes sufficiently confident model predictions are often correct. FixMatch uses a confident prediction on a weak augmentation as a target for a stronger augmentation. [1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2001.07685) [2](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/user_guide.html)

For an image, a mild crop may produce a reliable class estimate, and a stronger but label-preserving transformation should retain that class. If the transformation removes the only relevant object, the consistency target becomes wrong.

**Errors can reinforce themselves.** A confident mistaken pseudo-label becomes training evidence, making the next model even more confident in the mistake. Class imbalance can then starve minority classes of selected examples.

Use a trusted validation set, inspect class coverage, ramp the unlabeled-loss contribution, and consider class-aware sampling or thresholds. Check domain shift and graph quality. Confidence is produced by the same model being improved; it is not independent ground truth. Compare against a labeled-only baseline at equal compute to establish that the unlabeled pipeline actually helps.

**Technical details and references.**

Label propagation spreads labels through a similarity graph, assuming connected/high-density neighborhoods tend to share labels. Pseudo-labeling trains on the model's own confident predictions. FixMatch obtains a target from a weakly augmented unlabeled example and enforces it on a strongly augmented view when confidence exceeds a threshold. [1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2001.07685) [2](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/user_guide.html)

Confirmation bias appears when wrong but confident predictions become new training targets, particularly under class imbalance, domain shift, poor graph edges, or augmentations that change the label. Use a trusted validation set, calibration checks, class-aware thresholds or sampling, and a ramped unlabeled-loss weight. Monitor class coverage and error accumulation over iterations. More unlabeled data helps only when its structure and distribution support the assumptions; confidence is not an independent source of ground truth.
